info.title: graph8 Developer API
info.description: Public API for programmatic access to graph8 data. Authenticate with an org API key: `Authorization: Bearer <api_key>`

post.description:
PREVIEW. This endpoint is deployed but gated: it returns 404 unless the hosted app platform is enabled for your organization. It is published here so the contract describes the whole surface, not so it can be called today.

Mint a short-lived browser app token for the authenticated PropelAuth principal.

Auth is the EXISTING ``get_current_user`` PropelAuth dependency — no valid
principal -> 401. ``subject`` / ``client_org_id`` / ``role`` are derived
SERVER-SIDE from that validated principal (``derive_browser_identity``), never
from ``body`` — a forged identity/role in the body has no effect. Minting also
requires a consented installation of the target app in the principal's org (403).
A fail-closed per-principal / per-app limiter throttles the mint (429).

PREVIEW. This endpoint is deployed but gated: it returns 404 unless the hosted app platform is enabled for your organization. It is published here so the contract describes the whole surface, not so it can be called today.

Mint a service (client-credentials) app token bound to the credential's org.

A fail-closed per-credential limiter throttles the mint (429) before the
credential is even checked, so brute-forcing a client secret is rate-bound.

get.description:
Is this contact suppressed, and on which channel(s)?

Reads the SAME central ledger every send path checks
(``apps.suppression().service().list_suppressions``), so a "not
suppressed" answer here means the same thing it means to the sequencer
and newsletter send gates.

Paginated org-wide list of active suppressions.

Unlike the app's Data -> Suppressions grid (which joins contact/company
names for display), this is the raw ledger -- no PII, see module
docstring. Resolve a row's contact via ``GET /contacts/{contact_id}``.

post.description:
Stop all outreach to a contact. Proxies the SAME handler the in-app
contact view's "Suppress" action calls (``contacts/router.py:1660``) --
channel=all, category=org_initiated, honoured by every surface that
reads the central ledger (sequencer, newsletter, audience_sync).

Reverse an operator suppression. Proxies the SAME handler the in-app
contact view's "Unsuppress" action calls (``contacts/router.py:1702``).
Clears ONLY the org_initiated umbrella -- an independent
contact_initiated (they-asked) or system (bounce/complaint) opt-out is
never overridden through this endpoint, matching the app exactly.

Suppress an explicit set of contacts in one call. Proxies the SAME
handler the app's Lists -> add-to-suppressions bulk action calls
(``contacts/router.py:1819``), minus the list/filter-model resolution
(a UI concept) -- pass the contact PKs you already have. Idempotent:
already-active rows are left untouched.

Bulk-reinstate contacts. Proxies the SAME handler the app's
Suppressions grid "Reinstate" bulk action calls
(``contacts/router.py:1771``). ``operator_reversible`` is recomputed
server-side per contact; a contact whose only active suppression is
contact_initiated or system is skipped and reported, never reinstated.

get.description:
Every column the grid can show, with its type and display name.

The richest of the schema reads here: it carries base columns, custom
columns and enrichment columns together. `GET /contacts/columns` returns
the custom columns alone.

schema.description: Include the columns specific to this list. The list also decides whether contact or company columns are returned - a companies list returns company columns from this contacts path.

get.description:
The org's custom columns as `{column_id, name}` pairs.

The flat form: enough to build a field picker, and the source of the ids
other calls accept.

Which fields can be searched, and what each one COSTS.

Every entry carries a `tier` derived from the org's real indexes -
`fast`, `text_search` or `full_scan` - plus the operators that column's
live type supports. Index coverage is per-org, so this is the only honest
way to know a custom-column search is a full table scan before running it.

The real DATABASE columns behind a list.

Excludes the composite and enrichment columns the grid displays, so what
comes back is what can actually be written to and filtered on.

schema.description: Required: the list decides which base columns exist.
schema.title: List Id

get.description: Column names only, as a flat list of strings.

Fields grouped the way the contact form presents them.

Same underlying columns as the schema reads above, arranged into labelled
groups with a `required` flag - what to render, rather than what exists.

Counts and distributions across the contacts this key can see.

Scoped, not org-wide: a key narrowed away from contacts gets its own
narrower totals rather than the organisation's.

post.description:
Page through contacts, projecting only the columns you name.

A POST because the filter is a body, not because it writes: this reads and
mutates nothing, and is tiered as a read so a read-only key can call it.

Prefer this over `GET /contacts` when you want a narrow column set -
naming the columns lets the planner drop joins the full row forces.

Resolve profile photos for a batch of LinkedIn URLs.

A missing key in the result means "no allow-listed photo for that URL",
not "the lookup failed" - roughly half of contacts have one. Soft-fails to
an empty map rather than erroring, so it is safe on a render path.

Every column value for one row, resolved through a list.

The list is required, not optional: it decides whether `record_id` names a
contact or a company and which list-scoped custom columns apply. Reading
the same id through two different lists can legitimately return different
columns.

Apply a DIFFERENT change to each of many contacts.

The whole target set is authorised before the first write, so a batch
containing one contact the key cannot write is refused outright rather
than half-applied.

After that preflight, individual failures are REPORTED, not fatal: read
`updated`, `failed` and the per-contact `errors` rather than the HTTP
status.

schema.description: One object per contact. Each MUST carry `id`; every other key is a field to set on that contact.

post.description:
Set the owner on EVERY contact matching a selection.

The selection is resolved server-side, so the number of contacts affected
is not bounded by anything in the request. A null `owner_id` UNASSIGNS
them all.

Add every contact matching a filter into `target_list_id`.

Despite the name this does NOT merge duplicate contacts together - it
merges a SELECTION INTO A LIST. `/duplicates` is the surface that merges
records.

A 409 means some contacts need a decision before they can be added; re-send
with `conflict_resolution`. Blocked contacts are never added regardless.

Take contacts OUT of a sequence. They stop receiving its steps.

`remove_all=true` withdraws them from EVERY sequence they are enrolled in
and ignores `sequence_id` - the wider blast radius of the two, and never
the default.

`response` is REQUIRED by the app handler rather than decoration: it sets
a status on it for the partial-withdrawal case, so omitting it is an
AttributeError on every call.

Re-check deliverability for a batch of contacts. SPENDS CREDITS.

Synchronous: one call to the verification service, and the result is
written back onto each contact. Capped at 1000 contacts - use
`/contacts/verify-email/async` for a whole list.

Different from `POST /enrichment/verify-email`, which checks one arbitrary
address and stores nothing.

post.description:
Queue verification for a whole list or filtered selection. SPENDS CREDITS.

Returns the number of contacts and addresses ACCEPTED, not verified - the
results land on the contacts as the job runs. `all_matching` resolves the
selection server-side, so the cost is not bounded by anything in the
request; send the filter you actually mean.

Reveal withheld contact details. CHARGES CREDITS.

Returns `credits_charged`. Contacts already unlocked are not charged
again, so re-sending the same ids is safe - but `all_matching` resolves an
unbounded selection, and every newly-unlocked contact in it is billed.

How much this contact has engaged: emails, calls, meetings, visits.

Gated on `id_kind="pk"` because the handler counts against

a different row than it serves.
Pages this contact visited on your site.

get.description:
What to do next with this contact, and why. SPENDS CREDITS.

A GET that costs money: the recommendation is generated by a model on a
cache miss, and the cache key includes the contact's engagement state, so
activity on the record invalidates it. Tiered `billable` for that reason
rather than as an ordinary read - polling it per contact is real spend.

Everything the contact detail view shows, in one call.

Open-shaped: this is a composed view whose panels grow with the product.

Which workflows have run against this record, and what they produced.

Carries the execution timeline, each run's outputs, and the actions
currently available on the row. The workflow-permission gate is the app's
own, including its soak behaviour - while the enforcement flag is off a
caller without `workflows:read` is logged and allowed, because that
permission is not yet held by every role.

Under `/contacts/` because the record scope it enforces is the CONTACT
one, but `record_id` is whatever the list holds: a companies list reads
company rows through this path.

schema.description: Required: the list the record is read through.

post.description:
Generate the full document set for this contact. SPENDS CREDITS.

Enqueues the work and returns immediately; poll
`/contacts/{contact_id}/documents/generation-status` for progress. Each
document is a model call, so calling this repeatedly on the same contact
spends repeatedly.

get.description:
Progress of this contact's document generation. Reads only.

Named for the app route it proxies, which means the path contains
`generate` - the tier heuristic reads that as an active GET and would
publish a status poll as a credit spend. It is corrected by an explicit
entry in `build_scope_policy.py::READ_ONLY_ACTIVE_GET_ROUTES` rather than
by spelling the path around the matcher.

post.description: Store a skill run's output on this contact as a document.

get.description:
One timeline over everything that happened to a record.

Replaces four separate per-type reads. `entity_type` decides which record
scope authorises the call, and all four are resolved from the CALLING
KEY'S OWN credential scopes - so a key without `deals:read` resolves the
deal scope to nothing and cannot read a deal's feed through this path,
even though the key gate on the route is `contacts:read`.

post.description:
Dry-run a duplicate-detection rule. Writes nothing.

Returns the pair count the rule would match plus a small sample, which is
the only way to size a rule before auto-merge acts on it. A POST because
the rule is a body; tiered a read so a read-only key can check a rule
before someone saves it.

Run auto-merge once. RECORDS ARE DESTROYED.

Each merge removes one record and moves its data onto the survivor. The
only way back is `POST /duplicates/undo-merge/{merge_history_id}`, one
merge at a time. Send `dry_run=true` first.

A 200 does NOT by itself mean anything merged: if the org has auto-merge
disabled or is in shadow mode the response says so instead of failing,
which is the app's behaviour and is preserved here. Read the body.

get.description:
How many companies and contacts are flagged as needing review.

ORG-WIDE counts. The app handler takes no record scope, so unlike the
listing beside it these totals are not narrowed to what the caller can
see - two keys with different record scopes get the same numbers.

Companies with their revenue and account overlays joined on.

`GET /companies` returns the base record. This returns the same companies
with the ABM and revenue overlay fields - tier, score, owner, status -
coalesced in, which is what the account views are built from.

Contacts across EVERY company, with their company and pipeline context.

The buying-committee view: `department`, `buying_role` and `in_pipeline`
are not available on `GET /contacts`, and each row carries the company it
belongs to.

Published under `/companies` because that is the surface it belongs to,
but the rows it returns are CONTACTS and it is filtered by the CONTACT
record scope. A key holding `companies:read` without contact visibility
resolves that scope to nothing and gets an empty result rather than a
company-scoped one - it fails closed, but it is worth knowing which of the
two scopes actually governs the rows.

post.description:
Create or update companies from a batch of contacts. SPENDS CREDITS.

Contacts are grouped by email domain: a new domain creates a company, a
known one is updated. Every NEW company then triggers the full
intelligence pipeline - a site crawl, several model calls and a paid
enrichment lookup - and every contact triggers a paid person lookup. One
request with 50 domains and 500 contacts is 50 pipelines plus 550 provider
calls, so this is the most expensive operation on the company surface.

The body is REQUIRED here. The app declares it optional and then reads
`data.contacts` unconditionally, so an empty request there is an
AttributeError and a 500; requiring it makes the same request a 422.

Individual rows can fail without failing the call - read the response
rather than the status.

Set the owner on EVERY company matching a selection.

The selection is resolved server-side, so the number of companies affected
is not bounded by anything in the request. A null `owner_id` UNASSIGNS
them all.

Add every company matching a filter into `target_list_id`.

Despite the name this does NOT merge duplicate companies together - it
merges a SELECTION INTO A LIST. `/duplicates` merges records.

A 409 means some companies need a decision; re-send with
`conflict_resolution`.

get.description:
Billing details discovered for this company, ready to prefill a quote.

`status` is the field to read first: `ready` means the details are usable,
`pending` means discovery has not finished, `empty` means nothing was
found. Reads only - it does not trigger discovery.

The people at this company, with their buying-committee roles.

Overlaps `GET /companies/{company_id}/contacts`, which returns the same
people as contact records. This one is the account-team view: the roles
and engagement scoring the ABM surface reads.
Where this company's intelligence and synthesis workflows stand.

parameters.name: include_documents

schema.description: Also list the documents each workflow produced.
schema.title: Include Documents

parameters.description: Also list the documents each workflow produced.

get.description:
Whether synthesis can run yet, and what is blocking it.

Worth calling before `retry-synthesis`: `blocking_issues` names what is
missing, and retrying without fixing it spends credits to fail again.

Per-step state of the intelligence pipeline for this company.

The granular view: one entry per step with its own status, progress and
error. `intelligence-status` is the single rolled-up answer.
One rolled-up status for this company's intelligence run.

Everything the company detail view shows, in one call.

The deal it surfaces is filtered by its own ALWAYS-ENFORCED deal scope:
being able to see a company never implies being able to see its deals, so
a key without deal visibility gets the dashboard with no active deal
rather than a deal it should not see.

Open-shaped, and it has three legitimate shapes - a full dashboard, and
two shells for companies that have not been through the account pipeline.
Read `document_status` to tell them apart.
How much this company has engaged: emails, calls, meetings, visits.
Pages people at this company visited on your site.

schema.description: Lookback window. Bounded here rather than left open: the query is an unindexed analytics scan and an unbounded window is a cheap way to exhaust it.
schema.title: Days

get.description:
How well this company matches your ideal-customer profiles.

A company with no match is a 404 here. The app handler answers 200 with an
`error` key instead, which makes a missing company indistinguishable from
a scored one at the status line - translated at this boundary rather than
published.

What to do next with this company, and why. SPENDS CREDITS.

A GET that costs money: the recommendation is generated by a model on a
cache miss, and the cache key includes the company's engagement state, so
activity on the account invalidates it. Tiered `billable` for that reason
rather than as an ordinary read.

post.description:
Look this company up with the enrichment provider. SPENDS CREDITS.

Queues the lookup and returns immediately; the fields land on the company
when it completes. A company with no domain is refused - the lookup is by
domain.

The app spells this route after the provider it happens to use today. That
name is not published here: which provider runs is an implementation
detail, and the route would have to be renamed the day it changes.

Re-run the intelligence pipeline for this company. SPENDS CREDITS.

A site crawl plus several model calls per document. Omitting `doc_types`
regenerates the DEFAULT set, so an empty body is the expensive option and
not the cheap one - name the documents you actually need.

A run stuck for more than half an hour is treated as abandoned and
restarted, so this is callable again rather than wedged, but that also
means it can be re-triggered on a cadence. It is tiered `billable`.

Re-run synthesis for this company. SPENDS CREDITS.

Check `synthesis-readiness` first: a run that is missing its inputs spends
the same credits to produce nothing. A synthesis already marked running is
refused with a 409 - unlike the intelligence retry beside it there is no
stale-run reset, so a genuinely stuck run needs support rather than a
retry loop.
Store a skill run's output on this company as a document.

put.description:
Edit a reply. AUTHOR ONLY.

An organisation key has no member identity, so it is not the author of
anything a human wrote and cannot edit those replies - it can edit the
ones it posted itself.

delete.description: Delete a reply. AUTHOR ONLY. The rest of the thread stays.

get.description:
The subtasks under one task, filtered by what this key can see.

A private subtask belonging to someone else is absent rather than
redacted, so a short list is not evidence there are no more.

post.description:
Create a subtask under this task.

`entity_type` / `entity_id` name the RECORD the subtask hangs off and are
required - the parent supplies the hierarchy, not the record link. That
record is authorised against the caller's contact, company and deal
scopes, so a subtask cannot be attached to something the key cannot see.

`parent_task_id` in the body is ignored: the parent is the task in the
path.

put.description:
Patch a subtask. Omitted fields are left alone.

Two exceptions worth knowing. An explicit `null` on `due_date`,
`assignee_id` or `task_type` CLEARS that field, which is different from
omitting it. And `records: []` clears every record link, while omitting
`records` leaves them unchanged.

`expected_updated_at` makes the update conditional: if the stored row has
moved on, the write is refused instead of overwriting someone else's edit.

delete.description: Delete one subtask. The parent and its siblings are untouched.

post.description:
Push this task's reminder out by N minutes FROM NOW.

Relative to the call, not to the existing reminder time, so snoozing an
overdue reminder by 30 moves it to half an hour from now rather than to
half an hour after a moment that has passed.

get.description: The thread under a task, plus its resolution row if it has one.

post.description:
Post a reply on this task's thread. INTERNAL to your organisation.

Nothing here reaches a customer. `mentioned_user_ids` notifies those
people inside graph8 - it does not email anyone outside it.

Mark this task's DISCUSSION resolved.

Not the same as completing the task: a task can be done with an open
thread, and a thread can be resolved while the task is still open.
Idempotent - re-resolving returns the existing row rather than a second
one.

delete.description:
Reopen this task's discussion. The replies were never deleted.

Spelled as a DELETE because what it removes is the RESOLUTION, not the
thread - this is the app's own spelling and the inverse of the POST above.

get.description:
The org's task settings: default visibility, mentions, and how a parent
task completes relative to its subtasks.

put.description:
Change how a parent task completes. ORG ADMIN ONLY.

The app gates this twice - `require_admin_access` on the route and an
owner/admin role check in the body. The route gate is re-declared here;
the body check reads the role off the principal `build_api_principal`
resolves from the validated key, so a machine key (no human, no role) is
refused exactly as the app would refuse a member.

get.description:
Resolve the record a task points at to its display name and link.

404 when the record does not exist or the key cannot see it. The task
scope resolved for an API key carries no `record_scopes`, so the key's
own resource grants (`get_task_record_scopes`, the same resolver
`GET /tasks/{task_id}` uses) are attached before the lookup.

put.description:
Edit a reply. AUTHOR ONLY.

An organisation key has no member identity, so it is not the author of
anything a human wrote - it can edit the replies it posted itself.

delete.description: Delete a reply. AUTHOR ONLY. The rest of the thread stays.

get.description: The thread under a note, plus its resolution row if it has one.

post.description:
Post a reply on this note's thread. INTERNAL to your organisation.

Nothing here reaches the contact the note is about. `mentioned_user_ids`
notifies those people inside graph8.

Write access is checked against the RECORD the note hangs off, not the
note: replying is a write to that record's collaboration surface.

Mark this note's discussion resolved.

Idempotent - re-resolving returns the existing row rather than creating a
second one. The replies are untouched.

delete.description:
Reopen this note's discussion. Nothing is deleted.

Spelled as a DELETE because what it removes is the RESOLUTION, not the
thread - the app's own spelling, and the inverse of the POST above. It is
a WRITE on the underlying record despite the verb, and the gate says so
explicitly rather than inferring it from the method.

get.description:
Every note on one record, including notes that only MENTION it.

The per-record reads (`GET /contacts/{id}/notes` and friends) return the
notes attached to the record; this one also follows secondary links, so a
note filed on a deal that names this contact appears here too.

post.description:
Create a note attached to one or MORE records.

With `records`, the first entry is the primary record and every entry is
linked; without it, `entity_type`/`entity_id` name the single record.
Every record is authorised for write before anything is stored.

The notes of many contacts in one read, grouped by contact. Writes nothing.

POST only because the id list is a body. Every contact is authorised first.
Also file this note under another record. Idempotent.

delete.description:
Stop filing this note under a record. The note itself is kept.

The app takes the record in a DELETE body; it is a query string here,
because a body on DELETE is dropped by many HTTP clients and proxies.
The app refuses to remove a note's LAST record, so a note never orphans.

put.description:
Mark the whole team's notifications for one record as READ.

The rows survive, stamped with who read them, so the bell can still show
that someone acknowledged it. Idempotent: only unread rows are touched.

Omitting `notification_type` is the wide option - it marks every
notification anyone in the org holds for that record, including mentions
that were meant for a person.

parameters.name: entity_type

schema.description: Record type the notification is about, e.g. `chat`.
schema.title: Entity Type

parameters.description: Record type the notification is about, e.g. `chat`.

parameters.name: notification_type

schema.description: Narrow to one notification type. Pass the type you own - omitting it also marks unrelated notifications on the same record, such as a colleague's mention.
schema.title: Notification Type

parameters.description: Narrow to one notification type. Pass the type you own - omitting it also marks unrelated notifications on the same record, such as a colleague's mention.

delete.description:
Delete the whole team's notifications for one record.

Removes the rows for every user in your organisation, not just the
caller's. There is no undo, and unlike the read marker above nothing
survives to show the notification existed - prefer
`PUT /notifications/by-entity/read` unless the notification was noise.

parameters.name: entity_type

schema.description: Record type the notification is about, e.g. `chat`.
schema.title: Entity Type

parameters.description: Record type the notification is about, e.g. `chat`.

parameters.name: notification_type

schema.description: Narrow to one notification type. Pass the type you own - omitting it also deletes unrelated notifications on the same record.
schema.title: Notification Type

parameters.description: Narrow to one notification type. Pass the type you own - omitting it also deletes unrelated notifications on the same record.

get.description:
How far the profile-building pipeline has got, card by card.

Four stages - intelligence gathering, the merge, approval, and the profile
itself - each with its own state, so a caller can tell "still crawling"
from "waiting for a human" from "done".

The `website_url` echoed back is the string you sent; the lookup itself is
done against its canonical domain, so a match on a differently-spelled URL
is expected rather than a mismatch.

parameters.name: website_url

schema.description: The website the profile was built from.
schema.title: Website Url

parameters.description: The website the profile was built from.

post.description:
Release a human's approval on the profile so it can be rewritten.

An approved profile is immutable through `PUT /company-profile` unless
that call is sent with `unapprove_if_approved`. This is the standalone
half: it clears the approval WITHOUT changing a field, which is what you
want when the approval was premature rather than the content wrong.

Org-wide and immediate. Nothing re-approves automatically.

Rebuild the search index over this profile. SPENDS PROVIDER BUDGET.

Every call re-embeds the whole profile through the embedding provider -

post.description:
What are these CRM companies hiring for, right now?

A growth/buying signal: a company staffing up is a company with budget.
Unrelated to `/marketplace/job-posts`, which publishes SDR roles you are
recruiting for - both are called "jobs" but they share no data.

`company_ids` are `mashup_companies.id` values, NOT `linkedin_company_id`.
Both are bare ints, so passing the wrong one addresses a different company
rather than erroring.

Results split into `items` (resolved) and `unresolved`. An unresolved
company is normal: it means the company could not be matched to a LinkedIn
company page, not that it is not hiring. Read `lcid_confidence` before
trusting a match - 1.0 is an exact LinkedIn-URL match, 0.7 is a domain
fallback that can mismatch on shared or parked domains. `open_jobs` counts
postings seen within `window_days`; the source carries no open/closed state,
so a filled role lingers until it ages out.

Org isolation is by Postgres schema, so ids belonging to another org come
back as `unresolved` with no existence disclosure. Owner-level RBAC
(`CompanyScopeFilter`) is deliberately not applied: it reads
`user.permissions`, which an API-key user does not carry, so wiring it in
would resolve every API-key caller to scope "none" and return zero rows.

post.description:
Stop paying for a purchased mailbox. STOPS SPEND; eventually destroys it.

Two steps, and this is the first: the mailbox is scheduled for
cancellation at the provider and keeps working until its current period
ends. A poller then flips it to cancelled, after which
`DELETE /mailboxes/{mailbox_id}` removes graph8's record of it.

Reversible with `POST /mailboxes/uncancel` while it is still scheduled -
which resumes billing.

422 for a mailbox that was not purchased through graph8, or one already in
the cancellation flow. 502 if the provider refused - read that as "nothing
was cancelled", not as a partial success.

Needs a personal API key whose user holds a mailbox write permission.

Undo a scheduled cancellation. RESUMES BILLING on every mailbox listed.

Bulk by design; pass one id for a single undo. Idempotent - a mailbox that
is already active is a no-op success rather than an error.

Read the per-id breakdown in `results`, not the HTTP status: a mailbox
that could not be restored is REPORTED, and the request still returns 200
with the ones that were.

422 for an org without an active or pre-funded plan. A churned org must
not resume mailbox billing, and restoring one would be re-cancelled within
days anyway.

Needs a personal API key whose user holds a mailbox write permission.

Let the rest of the org send from this mailbox, or stop letting them.

Sharing hands over a sending CREDENTIAL, not a view: anyone in the org can
then attach it to their own sequences. Explicit rather than a toggle, so a
retried request cannot silently flip it back.

Owner-only (plus org admins and owners) - sharing is the one mailbox
mutation a team-mate the mailbox is already shared with cannot perform.
Needs a personal API key.

Archive a mailbox, or restore it. Explicit rather than a toggle.

Archiving hides the mailbox from pickers so nothing new is attached to it;
it is not deleted, keeps its history, and `is_archived=false` brings it
back. It does not cancel a purchased mailbox's billing - that is
`request-cancellation`.

Needs a personal API key whose user holds a mailbox write permission.

202 means ACCEPTED, not imported: the work runs in the background and the
response carries no per-row outcome. Poll `GET /mailboxes` to see what
landed, and expect rows to appear gradually rather than all at once.

Credentials in the CSV are write-only - stored encrypted and never
returned by this or any other endpoint.

Run an inbox-placement test for ONE mailbox. THIS CHARGES CREDITS.

Same charging path as `POST /placement/tests`: credits are held and
charged when the test is CREATED, not when it completes. Call
`POST /placement/tests/estimate` first if you want the figure - that one
is free.

Backed by a single DB transaction with ONE view rebuild for the whole batch

Per-column `enrichment` blocks are applied AFTER the columns commit; if a
companion enrichment config fails for one column, that column still exists
and its `results[]` entry reports `ok=false` with the error — the rest of
the batch is unaffected (mirrors the single endpoint's column-then-config
ordering, but per-field instead of failing the whole request).

patch.description:
Write custom column values to one OR many rows in a single call.

The batch counterpart of ``PATCH /fields/{column_id}/values``. Each row
carries its own ``record_id`` and a list of ``{column_id, value}`` pairs;
every row shares the top-level ``entity``. A single-row update is just a
``rows`` list of length one.

Partial success: each row is applied inside its own SAVEPOINT, so a bad row
(missing record, unknown column) is reported ``ok: false`` in ``results[]``
while the remaining rows still commit. Pass ``value=null`` (or omit it) on a
pair to clear that column for the row.

Limits: 1-500 rows per call; a ``record_id`` may appear only once per call
(fold that record's writes into one row) - duplicates 400.

Efficiency: all referenced ``column_id``s are resolved in one query and all
``record_id``s are existence-checked in one query, then each row is written
with a single multi-column upsert (N+2 statements, not N*M).

Write a custom column value to a single contact or company row.

Resolves ``column_id`` to the underlying ``column_name_db`` from
``dynamic_columns``, then performs an ``INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE``
against ``mashup_contact_attrs`` (or ``mashup_company_attrs`` for companies).

Pass ``value=null`` (or omit it) to clear the column for that row.

Notes:
    - The column must exist in ``dynamic_columns`` (not soft-deleted) for
      this org and the matching entity. Returns 404 otherwise.
    - The record (contact or company) must exist - the underlying foreign
      key constraint enforces this; a missing record yields a 404.
    - Custom column writes do NOT trigger view recreation; only column
      creation does (see ``CdpMashupContactRepository.create_column``).

put.description:
Bind this app to the repository a build should fetch (J1).

Idempotent, and a REPLACE rather than a merge: every field is written, so
rebinding from one provider to another cannot leave the previous provider's
credential pointer behind. A build fetching a new repo with a stale
credential is the failure this shape exists to prevent.

There is no GET here on purpose. Source is 1:1 with the app and comes back on
`GET /apps/{app_id}` through `AppResponse`, so a separate read would be a
second thing to keep in step for no new information.

`credential_ref` is a POINTER to a secret, never a secret. The DTO says so and
the column comment says so, because a token written here would also live in
every backup of the control plane and in this route's own response.

delete.description:
Unbind this app's source.

Idempotent: unbinding an app that has no source is a 200 describing an app
with no source, not a 404. The caller asked for a state, and that state
already holds.

Clearing the binding does NOT touch deployments already built from it. A
deployment records what was built; rewriting history to match a since-removed
binding would make the audit trail lie about what is running.

get.description:
Which secrets this app declares, and where they live (M9 item J7).

POINTERS ONLY. There is no value in the response and no column that could
hold one: the platform stores which secrets an app declares so a build can be
rendered, without ever holding what the build will read.

A hosted app needs config -- its own API keys, a database URL, the graph8
credential it calls back with -- and there was no route, DTO or operation id
for any of it anywhere in the contract.

put.description:
Declare a secret, or rotate where an existing one lives.

UPSERT, not create. Re-declaring a key is a rotation rather than a 409: the
builder is saying the value moved, and refusing would make the common case an
error and push them towards delete-then-create, which loses `created_at` and
briefly leaves the app declaring nothing.

`provider_ref` is a POINTER. The DTO refuses the obvious credential shapes,
which is a guardrail against the honest mistake rather than a security
control: nothing can reliably tell a path from a secret, but someone pasting a
value because the field sits next to the key is the likely error, and this
turns a silent unrecoverable leak into a 422 they read.

delete.description:
Stop declaring a secret.

Removes the DECLARATION, not the value: the value lives in the secret manager
and this surface never had it to delete. A builder revoking a credential has
to do it there as well, which the description says so nobody assumes this call
was enough.

404 when the app declares no such key, so a typo is not reported as a
successful removal of something else.

get.description:
Can this app be built and run yet, and if not, what is missing (M9 J9).

ANSWERS FROM THE CONTROL PLANE, AND SAYS SO. It reports what graph8 has
recorded: a bound source, an assigned hostname, declared secrets, the last
deployment's state. It does NOT claim the cluster side is ready, because the
namespace provisioner, the image registry and the runtime objects are
separate, unbuilt work. Reporting `ready: true` on that basis would be the
most expensive kind of wrong: a builder would push and wait for something
nothing can serve.

`blockers` is the field that matters. An agent driving a build needs to know
WHY it cannot proceed; a bare `ready: false` sends it guessing, and guessing
against a deploy pipeline is how you get retry loops.

Deliberately cheap: three reads the caller could make themselves across
`GET /apps/{id}`, `/secrets` and `/deployments`. It exists so the answer is
computed in one place, because "am I ready" is a judgement about which
prerequisites matter, and three clients would each get it slightly wrong.

put.description:
PREVIEW. This endpoint is deployed but gated: it returns 404 unless the hosted app platform is enabled for your organization. It is published here so the contract describes the whole surface, not so it can be called today.

Set this app's hard credit cap for a window.

`set_limit` and `clear_limit` shipped with the repository layer
(`repositories/usage.py:198,229`), with a Protocol (`contracts.py:957`) and
tests, and NO route ever called them. So a builder could read their cap and
could never set one, and the only way a limit row came into existence was by
hand.

That matters more than a missing endpoint usually would: in a builder-pays
model the cap is the entire spend-safety story. Enforcement was complete and
unreachable.

Same shape as the #16816 bug, where `store_credential` and `revoke_credential`
shipped without callers so no service token could ever be minted.

SINGULAR `/limit`, not `/limits`. The read half is singular and is frozen
that way in `openapi_operation_ids.json` and the published bundle; adding a
plural verb would put two spellings of one resource in the public contract
forever.

A DELETE rather than `PUT {"credit_cap": 0}`, because absence of a row IS
"no cap" (`contracts.py:655`) and zero is a real cap meaning "allow nothing".
Collapsing the two would make an accidental zero indistinguishable from
uncapped, in the one place where guessing wrong costs money.

Idempotent: clearing an app that has no cap succeeds.

The target organization must already have a **consented** installation of
this app. A credential for a workspace that never consented would be a
standing key into a tenant that never agreed to it, and the M6-1d clamp would
refuse every request it minted anyway — failing here says why, instead of
leaving a credential that silently cannot work.

delete.description:
PREVIEW. This endpoint is deployed but gated: it returns 404 unless the hosted app platform is enabled for your organization. It is published here so the contract describes the whole surface, not so it can be called today.

Revoke a service credential. A status flip, never a delete.

Deleting would erase the evidence that the credential ever existed, which is
precisely what an incident review needs. Tokens already minted from it are
NOT retroactively invalid — they expire on their own short TTL — but no new
one can be minted.

post.description:
Validate a `graph8.app.yaml` without applying it. No app id needed.

Answers 200 whether or not the manifest is valid: the question "is this
valid" was served correctly even when the answer is no, and a 422 would make
a builder's linter treat a working call as a transport failure. `valid` is
the answer; `issues` carries every problem at once, each with a path pointer,
so a whole file is fixed in one round trip.

Requires an allowlisted builder org but no app, because linting a manifest
in CI should not require naming an app or holding a credential scoped to one.

Apply a `graph8.app.yaml` to this app.

Publishes the `objects:` block as a schema version through the same path
`POST /{app_id}/schema-versions` uses, including the digest idempotency and
the failure-isolated tenant fan-out, and stores `frontend:` / `backend:` as
the build config a later deploy reads.

Refuses when the manifest's `app.slug` names a DIFFERENT app than the one in
the path. Both halves of that mismatch are plausible mistakes -- a copied
file, a wrong id in a script -- and either one silently applied would
publish one app's schema into another app's tenants.

A manifest with no `objects:` publishes nothing. That is not an oversight:
an empty schema would archive every object the app has ever declared across
every consented tenant, so `schema_publish` refuses it, and a build-config
only manifest is a legitimate thing to apply.

Publish a declared object schema and materialize it across consented tenants.

422 with every validation problem at once, so a builder fixes their whole
schema in one round trip rather than one error per attempt.

A publish that resolves to an EXISTING version still returns 201 with
`created: false` -- the resource named by the response exists either way, and
the flag is what tells a caller nothing changed.

get.description:
Every schema version for this app, oldest ordinal first.

Includes drafts and deprecated versions. A builder asking "what did I ship
and when" needs the whole history, and a filtered list would make a
deprecated version look deleted.

post.description:
Create a page over one or more data sources.

Every source is validated against the connector registry BEFORE anything is
persisted, so a page can never reference a source that cannot be read.
422 names the offending source rather than failing generically later.

get.description: Your organization's app pages, most recently updated first.
One page and its bound sources.

delete.description:
Delete a page. Its sources and version history go with it.

A real delete, unlike most of the app platform: a page is the builder's own
generated artifact rather than a record of something that happened, so there
is no audit reason to keep a tombstone.

post.description:
Generate the page from its sources. Asynchronous; poll `/status`.

Billed, and rate-capped per organization per day. The ordering behind this
(re-authorize every source before spend, consume the cap, mark generating,
enqueue, refund and mark failed on error) is shared with the internal surface
rather than reimplemented here.

404 covers both an unknown page and a source that has become unreachable
since the page was created. Distinguishing them would let a caller probe
which sources exist.

get.description:
Is the page built yet?

`has_page` is separate from `status` because a page can be `ready` with no
stored HTML, and treating that as ready sends a viewer to an empty frame.

The generated HTML and the manifest wiring it to its sources.

This is the source, for reading or storing. To DISPLAY a page, mint a frame
session instead: the HTML is written for a sandboxed origin with an injected
SDK and is not safe to embed directly in your own document.

post.description:
Change the page by describing the change. Billed and rate-capped.

An edit that would strip every live-data binding is refused: a page whose
data wiring is gone renders stale markup that still looks live, which is
worse than a failed edit. Each accepted edit snapshots a new version.

get.description: Every stored version of this page, with the instruction that produced it.

post.description:
Restore an earlier version.

Restoring SNAPSHOTS rather than rewinds: the current page becomes a new
version before the old one is applied, so a restore is itself undoable and
nothing is destroyed.

Mint a one-shot token for loading this page's sandboxed frame.

The generated HTML is not safe to embed in your own document: it is written
for an isolated, cookieless origin under a `default-src 'none'` policy with
an injected data SDK. Load the returned `frame_url` in an iframe instead.

Single use and short lived, by design. A token that could be replayed would
be a bearer credential for the page's data, so each load mints a new one.

get.description:
What this page can do, grouped by the alias each action acts on.

A source that no longer authorizes contributes nothing rather than failing
the whole listing: one revoked binding should not make a page's other
actions undiscoverable.

post.description:
Invoke a declared action on one of this page's bound sources.

The bound source is RE-AUTHORIZED on every invocation, not just when the
page was created, so a source revoked since then stops accepting writes
immediately rather than at the next regeneration.

`404` covers an unknown page, an alias this page does not bind, and a source
that is no longer reachable. They are indistinguishable on purpose: telling
a caller which of the three it was lets a page enumerate what exists.

get.description:
Everything needed to render one session from cold.

THREE sources in one answer, and the difference between them matters:
`messages` are the chat bubbles, `steps` are what the agent actually did
(tool calls, reasoning summaries) and `work_item_status` is whether it is
still going. A session driven by a work item has richer `steps` than
`messages`, and a plain chat has only `messages` - so a client that renders
only one of them will show an empty conversation for half the sessions.

404s on a session the caller cannot see, rather than 403 - existence is not
leaked by distinguishing the two.

put.description:
Mark messages read up to a COUNT, not a flag.

A count higher than the session actually holds is refused with 409 rather
than accepted. That looks strict until you consider what accepting it does:
a stale client claiming to have read eleven messages when there are nine
would mark the next two read before anyone saw them, and the customer would
never be told the agent had replied.

The app answers 204 with no body; this returns the usual envelope so a
generated SDK has one response shape across the surface.

get.description:
Can this workspace use voice at all, and what does it cost.

The org-wide answer, with indicative pricing - ask this before building a
voice affordance into a UI. The per-session twin
(`GET /agent/sessions/{session_id}/voice`) answers the same question for one
conversation and additionally checks the caller owns it.

`available: false` comes with a `reason`, so a client can say WHY rather
than hiding the control.

post.description:
Create an EMPTY session to speak into.

It creates only the conversation - never a synthetic opening turn from the
agent. That is deliberate in the app and worth preserving: a fabricated
first message would appear in the transcript as something the agent said
when it had not yet heard anything.

`session_id` is caller-generated, so a client can open its socket and
create the row without a round trip between the two. Sending the same id
twice does not create a second session.

get.description:
Can voice be used on THIS session.

Differs from the workspace answer by also checking the caller owns the
session, so it is the one to ask before showing a microphone on a specific
conversation.

post.description:
Start speaking with the agent. THIS SPENDS CREDITS AS IT RUNS.

A live metered session: it begins charging when it connects and keeps
charging until it is ended or hits `max_credits`. Quote it first.

`max_credits` is a HARD CEILING and is required - there is no default,
because choosing one would mean this contract picking a spending limit on
the customer's behalf. `rate_version` must be the one the quote returned.

End it with `DELETE /agent/sessions/{session_id}/voice/{voice_id}`. A
session left open keeps costing money.

What a voice session WOULD cost. Charges nothing.

A POST only because the ceilings are a body. It returns a credit figure and
a `rate_version`, and that version is the point: hand it straight to
`POST /agent/sessions/{session_id}/voice`, which refuses a stale one rather
than starting at today's price against yesterday's quote.

Tiered as a READ for that reason. It is the only way to learn the price
before committing to it, so a read-only key must be able to call it.

delete.description:
Stop a live voice session, and stop the meter.

This is the one that costs money NOT to call. Ending is the only thing that
stops the charge short of the ceiling, so treat it as part of the start
call rather than as cleanup.

The CONVERSATION survives - this ends the audio session, not the chat. The
transcript stays readable through `GET /agent/sessions/{session_id}/state`.

parameters.name: voice_id

schema.description: Voice session id (UUID) from the start call.
schema.title: Voice Id

parameters.description: Voice session id (UUID) from the start call.

post.description:
Say something to the agent and get its answer.

`kind` in the answer says which way the turn went: `chat` is a reply in
`message`; `work_item` means the agent read the message as a job and
STARTED it - `work_item_id` is the work item, and whether its workflow
actually launched is in `workflow_started`.

Each turn runs a model and is charged. Omit `session_id` to start a new
session.

Append a message to an agent session WITHOUT asking for a reply.

No model runs and nothing is charged: the message is stored in the
session's log and shown to anyone watching it. Use `POST /agent/chat` to
get an answer. A session you cannot see is a 404.

get.description:
What your agents need from a person, and what they did without asking.

Three groups in one read: `approvals` (work stopped on a decision - each
row carries what `POST /agent/approvals/{approval_id}/decide` needs),
`blockers` (work stopped for another reason, with why) and
`autonomous_fixes` (changes made on your behalf).

AN EMPTY GROUP SAYS WHY. Read `states`: `ready` means the read worked and
there is nothing, `unavailable` means the read failed, `not_recorded`
means nothing is ever recorded there for this org (no skill is dialled to
act on its own). Every group is capped at `limit` and says so in `bounds`.

parameters.name: fix_window_hours

schema.description: How far back autonomous fixes are read.
schema.title: Fix Window Hours

parameters.description: How far back autonomous fixes are read.

post.description:
Answer a confirm card the agent posted into a session.

Onboarding runs stop on these ("is this your company?", "are these your
competitors?") and resume when the answer lands, usually within ten
seconds. Idempotent for the same `state`.

parameters.name: card_id

schema.description: The card's id in the session.
schema.title: Card Id

parameters.description: The card's id in the session.

post.description:
Open a Copilot session already briefed on one buyer-intent keyword.

Returns `session_id`. The session is seeded with the keyword's detail (and
the company or contact, if given), so the first question can be about it
without restating it. No model runs here.

get.description: Sessions owned by, or shared with, the principal behind this key.

post.description: Open a session, optionally seeded with messages.

get.description: Read one session, including its messages.

patch.description: Append messages or change the title. Omitted fields are untouched.

delete.description: Delete a session. Owner only - the internal handler enforces that.

post.description: Pin or unpin a session. Owner only.
Rename a session. Owner only.

Start a unit of autonomous work. THE AGENT BEGINS PLANNING IMMEDIATELY.

`agent_id` selects the planner template. A known id gets its own template;
anything else falls back to `full`, which is why it is an open string
rather than an enum - an enum would reject the ad-hoc case the planner
explicitly supports.

`visibility` defaults to `private`: work started through a key is not
visible org-wide unless asked for.

`user_email` defaults to the identity the key was minted under, so the item
belongs to a real person rather than to nobody.

get.description: Work items the caller can see.

parameters.name: statuses

schema.description: Status filter, REPEATABLE: `?statuses=running&statuses=queued`. Repeated rather than comma-joined, matching the app - a comma in a status would otherwise split it.
schema.title: Statuses

parameters.description: Status filter, REPEATABLE: `?statuses=running&statuses=queued`. Repeated rather than comma-joined, matching the app - a comma in a status would otherwise split it.

parameters.name: include_shared

schema.description: Include org-wide shared items as well as the caller's own. True by default, matching the app - set false to see only your own.
schema.title: Include Shared

parameters.description: Include org-wide shared items as well as the caller's own. True by default, matching the app - set false to see only your own.

post.description:
Redirect a RUNNING work item at its next safe step boundary.

Not mid-step - that is what makes steering safe at all. The instruction is
picked up when the agent reaches a boundary, so a steer sent during a long
tool call lands afterwards rather than corrupting it.

SAFE TO RETRY: `client_turn_id` is a caller-generated idempotency key, and
the same id twice comes back `status: "duplicate"` rather than queueing a
second instruction into a running agent. Check that field before assuming
a retry did something.

Stop a work item.

Stops the LOOP. Anything the agent already did - a sequence launched, a
record written - stays done; cancelling is not an undo.

get.description:
What the agent has learned and carries between sessions.

Returned open-shaped: memory is planner state that changes as the platform
does, and on an oversight surface a dropped field reads as an agent knowing
less than it does.

Where the agent was overruled, and on what.

The oversight signal worth acting on: it shows which of the agent's
suggestions humans rejected, which is how a customer tunes it rather than
turning it off.

What the agent would open a conversation with, unprompted.

A read - it computes a suggestion and starts nothing.

post.description:
Record which product the customer signed up for. FIRST WRITER WINS.

The entry point maps 1:1 to a plan template, so it chooses what the agent
proposes doing first. It is a one-shot ATTRIBUTION, not a settable
preference: if the org already has one, this call changes nothing and
reports the existing value.

Read `captured` rather than the status code - a 200 with `captured: false`
means someone else got there first, which is a normal outcome and not an
error.

Record first-touch attribution - UTM tags, ad click ids, landing page.

FIRST WRITER WINS on every key, so this is safe to call once per session
and safe to retry. Nothing already captured is overwritten.

Every field is optional, which means an empty body is legal and does
nothing. The response reports each destination separately
(`organization_persisted`, `contact_persisted`, ...) because attribution
lands in more than one place and a partial write is worth knowing about -
`complete` is the single field that says all of them took.

Answer the agent's "is this your company domain?" card.

`domain` is REQUIRED when `confirmed` is false and ignored when it is true.
The app enforces that with a 422 of its own, and this mirrors the model
rather than the check, so a missing domain is refused by the handler with
its own message rather than by a copy here that could drift.

A corrected domain is persisted immediately, so a late edit is not orphaned
once the polling activity has already exited.

Post ONE batched summary of what finished while the customer was away.

IDEMPOTENT by watermark: a marker on the previous catch-up message is the
high-water mark, so a repeat call posts nothing and comes back
`posted: false`. Below the app's minimum card count it is also a no-op - a
single completed card does not need a summary.

get.description:
The whole discovery record, plus an honest coverage report.

EVERY field comes back, answered or not - an unanswered one carries
`status: "open"` rather than being absent, so a caller renders a stable
list instead of one that grows as the interview proceeds.

`coverage` is the part worth reading: `open_musts` names what still blocks
a launch, `amber_fields` names the working assumptions, and `can_launch` is
the single boolean. It is not a percentage, on purpose - a framework with
silent gaps is worse than no framework, because the gaps become confident
copy three weeks later.

post.description:
Start the interview: show what the agent already worked out, and ask
where it is wrong.

Takes no body. Degrades gracefully when nothing is readable yet - a
brand-new org's site scrape lands minutes after signup, and the app decided
a routing question is a better opener than a spinner.

A VIEW never enrols an org into a kickoff: proposals are only STAGED for an
org that already has an onboarding room, which is what stops one visit
giving an established org a permanent door onto an empty conversation.

Correct what the agent inferred. The customer's word wins over the scrape.

`edits` overrides a value; `confirmed` accepts one as read. Both default to
empty, so ratifying nothing is a legal no-op rather than a 422 - which is
what makes the call safe to retry.

The response echoes PROGRESS, not the field list: `fields` comes back empty
by design because the caller already holds it from `GET /discovery`.

Record ONE graded answer.

`grade` is not decoration. A `red` grade stores NO VALUE and burns a rung of
the probe ladder - the agent asks again a different way rather than keeping
a guess. Storing an unusable answer as data is how a confident, wrong ICP
gets built.

`field_key` must be a real framework field; anything else is refused by the
handler by name rather than being written as a stray key.

One conversational turn of the kickoff. THIS ONE COSTS MONEY.

The only route on this surface that makes an LLM call, which is why it is
tiered `billable` and why the app rate-limits it at 20 requests a minute
per organisation - far above a human conversation, far below anything that
shows up on a bill. Over that, the app answers 429 with `Retry-After`.

The model replies AND states what it learned in one forced tool call, so a
message that answers four questions records four fields. Everything it
claims is validated before it is written: a key outside the framework is
dropped, and a `green` with no supporting quote is DOWNGRADED to `amber`
rather than trusted.

The turn writes only to the discovery record. It provisions nothing, calls
no tools, and sends nothing.

There is no `history` parameter and that is deliberate - see the module
docstring.

Create the global custom column behind each observable trigger.

Takes no body. A signal is defined ONCE for the account and every list
patches the same column - that is what makes cross-campaign analysis
possible at all, and why the column is global rather than list-scoped.

Triggers nothing can observe come back as `research` rather than being
quietly created: they are real and useful, but they belong in the copy
rather than in the targeting. Promising to watch something nothing watches
is a program that never fires and a failure nobody can see.

Turn the interview into real objects: an ICP, a persona, AND A CAMPAIGN.

Takes no body. The campaign is the part that surprises people, so it is
said plainly: this CREATES a campaign and provisions its Work channel. It
does not SEND anything - the campaign sits there for a human to launch -
which is why this is a `write` and not an `external` operation.

IDEMPOTENT: the projection is idempotent by object name, and the build is
claim-fenced, so calling twice updates the same ICP and returns the same
campaign rather than minting a second one.

PARTIAL SUCCESS IS A REAL OUTCOME. A refused build does not fail the
projection, because the ICP and persona are committed by the time the build
runs and reporting the whole call as failed would send someone to re-run a
projection that worked. Read `campaign.ok` in the body; a blocked build
names what is still open rather than counting it.

get.description:
The closing report: what is filled, which MUSTs are still open, what was
inferred rather than answered.

Deliberately not a score. The inferred fields are flagged rather than
counted, because the useful question at the end of an interview is "what
did we make up", not "how far did we get".

The campaign brief the record would produce. A PREVIEW - it writes
nothing.

Deterministic and LLM-free: running it again after two more answers gives
the same document plus two facts, not a differently-worded one. That is
what makes it safe to poll while the interview is still going.

It never fills a gap to look finished. `open_musts` and `assumptions` come
back alongside the copy, because a brief that reads as complete while four
must-answer questions are open is how a silent gap becomes a confident
wrong campaign.

Every operator on the bench, with whether it is switched on for you.

The starting point for this surface: it carries each operator's catalog
metadata and its live status - enabled, whether it has ever run, and how
many findings it is holding.

One digest across the whole bench.

Finding counts here are DISTINCT, not the sum of the per-operator numbers
from `GET /agent/operators`. Shared findings legitimately appear in several
operators' caches, and adding the cards up counts them more than once - the
app's own banner did exactly that before this was split out.

The organisation's operating model: which motions it runs, so operators
know what "normal" looks like here.

Read this before writing it. The write is a whole-document replace.

put.description:
Replace the organisation's operating-model override. PUT SEMANTICS.

The whole document is replaced: a key absent from `override` is REMOVED,
not left alone, and an empty object resets the org to graph8's defaults.
That is the app's behaviour and this does not soften it - a partial-update
spelling here would make the same body mean two different things on two
surfaces.

This is a policy document, not a switch, which is why it is tiered `write`
while `/enabled` is not: it describes the org, and an operator has to be
turned on separately before anything reads it unattended.

get.description:
Where operator approval tasks come from.

The vocabulary behind `GET /agent/operators/{operator}/findings` - what
kinds of thing raise an approval in the first place.

get.summary: Get Agent Operator For Approval Task
get.description:
Which operator raised this approval task.

The bridge between an approval sitting in someone's queue and the operator
whose dial produced it - so a caller can look at the right scorecard before
deciding, and can leave feedback against the right operator afterwards.
Is this operator on, and has it ever run.

This operator's snapshot of the organisation it watches.

Open-shaped: each operator reports the checks IT runs, and the set grows
with the product. A pinned mirror would silently drop a check, and on a
health surface a missing check reads as a passing one.
Everything this operator is CAPABLE of, whether or not it is enabled.

The action descriptors behind this operator's skills.

Static and org-independent - the same answer for every organisation. It is
the definition of what each action does and how reversible it is, which is
what the trust-dial ceiling is computed from.

The knowledge collections this operator reasons from.

Slug, name and a one-line summary only. The BODIES are never returned -
they are graph8-managed and locked, and the app does not expose them
either. This is not a gap in the proxy.

Has this operator been right, per skill.

The number to read before raising a dial. Raising autonomy on a skill with
a bad scorecard is how unattended work becomes unattended damage.

What this operator actually DID - decided approvals and remediations.

Findings are what it saw; this is what it changed. The audit trail for
unattended work, and the only place that distinguishes the two.

parameters.name: limit

schema.description: How many history rows to return. The app's own default is 50 and it declares no ceiling; a bound is added here because an unbounded limit on a public contract is a denial-of-service parameter.
schema.title: Limit

parameters.description: How many history rows to return. The app's own default is 50 and it declares no ceiling; a bound is added here because an unbounded limit on a public contract is a denial-of-service parameter.

get.description:
Which records one activity entry touched.

The row-level detail behind a single thing the operator did: what it
changed, not just that it changed something.

parameters.name: task_id

schema.description: Task id from the activity list.
schema.title: Task Id

parameters.description: Task id from the activity list.

get.description: What people have said about this operator, in aggregate.

put.description:
Switch this operator on or off for the organisation.

TURNING IT ON STARTS UNATTENDED WORK. The operator's monitors begin running
on their own schedule, without anyone asking, and they keep running until
this is set back to false. That is why this needs the `run` grant rather
than plain write: "let something act in my org when I am not watching" is
not the same permission as "edit a record".

What it is allowed to DO once it is on is a separate control - see
`PUT /agent/operators/{operator}/skills/{skill_key}`. Enabling an operator
whose skills are all `OFF` starts nothing.

`enabled` is explicit rather than a toggle, so a retried request is
idempotent instead of switching it back off.

get.description:
Each skill this operator has, and how far it may currently go.

The source of the `skill_key` values the trust-dial write accepts, and the
place to read back what a dial actually RESOLVED to after the risk cap was
applied.

put.description:
Set how far ONE skill may go on its own. THIS GOVERNS UNATTENDED ACTION.

The trust dial is the control that decides whether a finding stays a
finding, becomes an approval a person decides, or is simply DONE. Raising
it is the single most consequential write on this surface, which is why it
takes the `run` grant rather than plain write.

THE DIAL IS A CEILING REQUEST, NOT A SETTING. The effective autonomy is the
minimum of this value, the skill's graph8-managed risk cap and the platform
ceiling, so a skill capped at `PROPOSE` stays at `PROPOSE` no matter what
is sent. Read the response rather than assuming the write took literally.

Read `GET /agent/operators/{operator}/scorecard` first. A dial raised on a
skill that has been wrong is how unattended work becomes unattended damage.

get.description: Who currently receives this operator's alerts and owns its approvals.

put.description:
Name the person who owns this operator's approvals.

REPLACES the current recipient - there is one per operator, not a list.
Worth setting before enabling anything at `PROPOSE`, because an approval
task with no owner is an operator that has stopped.

post.description:
Approve or reject a fix this operator proposed.

`approved` RUNS THE FIX: the operator executes its proposed remediation
against your data, then records the result. `rejected` records the
decision and runs nothing. Needs OPERATOR_MANAGE, the same governance gate
as the trust dials, because this authorises execution.

A task that is not an open approval for this operator is a 404.

Send the agent back to replan, with a reason. THIS REJECTS THE PROPOSAL.

Not a "hold" and not a comment: the current proposal is rejected
ATOMICALLY, and the feedback is stored alongside so the next plan is
informed rather than identical. If you want the plan to proceed, use
`POST /agent/approvals/{approval_id}/decide`.

It FAILS CLOSED on both halves. A deployment that does not have this route
404s rather than doing something approximate, and a worker that does not
understand the stored feedback still reads the row as a rejection. There is
no version of "older software saw this as approval".

Once decided, an approval cannot be decided again - the winner is settled
server-side, so a second call gets 409 rather than overwriting.

get.description:
The sub-agents available to be delegated to.

The bench: who each specialist is, what it is for, and whether it backs the
Chief of Staff. Static and the same for every organisation - it is the
catalogue of what the platform can delegate to, not what YOUR org has
configured.

Read it to learn the `agent_id` values `POST /agent/work-items` accepts as
its planner template. An unknown id there falls back to the general planner
rather than failing, which is why that field is an open string - this is the
list that stops a caller relying on that fallback by accident.

post.description:
Resolve an @-mention: what can be referred to in a message to the agent.

Searches people, campaigns, accounts and documents in one call and returns
them with a `category`, so a composer can render one picker instead of four.
A read - it finds things, it changes nothing, and it starts no agent.

A POST only because the filter set is a body. `query` defaults to empty,
which returns the default suggestions rather than nothing, matching the app.

The app publishes the SAME search at `/v1/copilot/mention-search` from a
second router that lazily imports this one's helpers. One is enough on a
versioned contract, and this is the one under `/agent`, beside the sessions
the mentions are typed into.

get.description:
Pending approvals this key may act on.

An approval is the loop asking permission before it runs a tool. Each entry
carries the `plan_digest` it is bound to and its `expires_at`, so a caller
can tell an approval that still describes the plan from one that has drifted.

Decided approvals, newest first, same shape as the pending list.

Registered ABOVE `/approvals/{approval_id}/receipts` so the literal
`history` segment cannot be captured as an `approval_id`. `GET
/workflows/dispositions` 404'd in production for exactly that reason until
2026-08-07; the ordering here is load-bearing, not cosmetic.

parameters.name: decision

schema.description: Optional filter on the recorded decision: 'approve', 'reject', 'edit_and_approve' or 'dismiss'. An unrecognised value is rejected with 422 rather than silently ignored.
schema.title: Decision

get.description:
Signed provenance receipts attributed to one approval.

404 rather than 403 when the approval belongs to another tenant or to
another user's private work item: existence never leaks across that
boundary. Degrades to an empty list on a schema predating the receipt
columns rather than 500ing.

post.description:
Approve, reject, or edit-and-approve a pending approval.

Use `{decision, edit_payload}` for the existing decision mode, or exclusively
`{use_human_authorization: true}` to relay a short-lived decision previously
reviewed in the browser by the same personal-key owner. The relay accepts
no caller-authored decision or edit fields. There is no client
version to pass: double-decide is settled server-side by `WHERE decided_at
IS NULL`, so exactly one caller wins and the loser gets 409 rather than
overwriting the first decision.

`DecideRequest` does not forbid unknown keys, so a misspelled `edit_payload`
is dropped in silence and an `edit_and_approve` decides as a plain approve.
This docstring is the operation description in the published contract, so
getting it wrong here ships the wrong shape to every integrator generating a
client from the spec, which is exactly how the earlier `expected_version` /
`edited_payload` error nearly shipped.

Start a durable agent run.

"Run" is the public noun; the stored row is a work item and every internal
name says so. The same translation `app_pages_router` makes for dashboards,
and for the same reason: the public contract should read the way a builder
thinks, not the way the table is named.

`workflow_started: false` is a NORMAL outcome, not an error. The row is
persisted either way; a false means the Temporal worker did not pick it up
on this attempt and the reason is carried alongside it.

get.description:
List runs this key can see: its own, plus org-wide shared ones.

Reconciles abandoned rows before reading, so a run whose worker was recycled
reports `failed` rather than sitting at `running` forever.

parameters.name: include_shared

schema.description: When true (default), include org-wide shared runs. When false, return only runs this key owns.

get.description:
Fetch one run.

THE ONE ROUTE HERE THAT IS NOT PURE DELEGATION, because there is no
`GET /v1/agent/work-items/{id}` on the JWT surface to call. Without it a
builder can create a run, receive its id, and then have no way to poll it
except by listing everything and filtering client-side.

Its visibility rule is copied from `list_work_items`, NOT from
`cancel_work_item`: a read may see the caller's own runs plus org-wide
`visibility='shared'` ones, whereas cancel is owner-only because stopping
someone else's work is destructive. Pinning the read to the stricter rule
would hide a shared run that the list route shows, and the two disagreeing
about the same row is worse than either answer alone.

404, never 403, on a run the caller may not see: a non-owner must not be
able to use this route to probe which runs exist in the org. Same reason
`cancel_work_item` returns 404 for a non-owner.

post.description:
Stop a run and everything it spawned.

OWNER ONLY, and that is stricter than the read routes on purpose: shared
visibility lets an org SEE a teammate's run, while stopping it is
destructive and not undone by restarting. Children are signalled before the
root so a freed parent cannot leave orphans behind it.

Idempotent on an already-terminal run: `cancelled: false` with a reason,
not an error, so a double call does not look like a failure.

get.description: Every deployment for this app, newest first.

post.description:
Queue a deployment from a pinned source ref.

Returns `queued`. Nothing builds yet -- the provisioner (M6-8) is what moves
it to `building`. Recording the intent before any infrastructure exists is
deliberate: it makes the control plane the source of truth for what SHOULD be
running, which is what a reconciler needs to exist against.

get.description:
What is serving traffic right now, or null.

null rather than 404 when nothing is deployed: "this app has never shipped"
is an answer, and a 404 would read as "no such app".

Fetch one deployment.

Polling a build is the most common loop in a deploy flow, and without this it
required listing every deployment and filtering client-side.

REGISTERED AFTER `GET /{app_id}/deployments/active`, and the order is
load-bearing rather than cosmetic. Both are three segments with a literal or a
parameter in the same position, so declaring this first would capture `active`
as a deployment id and that endpoint would 404 for everyone. `GET
/workflows/dispositions` spent months doing exactly that in production.

404 rather than 403 for a deployment belonging to someone else's app, because
a 403 confirms the id exists. `_own_deployment` is the only way this module
loads one, so a new route cannot skip the ownership check without also having
nothing to work with.

post.description:
The build controller reports progress. THE KEYSTONE (M9 item J2).

Without this, every deploy route below is inert. `POST /deployments` writes
`queued`, and the state machine allows `queued -> building -> promoting ->
deployed`. Nothing anywhere wrote `building` or `promoting`, so promote asked
for `queued -> deployed`, which is illegal, and **every real deployment that
has ever existed 409s on promote** while `deployments/active` returns null for
every builder.

AUTHENTICATED AS THE CONTROLLER, NOT THE BUILDER, and that is the whole point.
A builder's own key must not be able to walk their deployment to `promoting`
with no build having run, then promote it: the machine would read green and
the image would be whatever was there before, or nothing. So this route takes
no `user` at all. See `dependencies/build_controller_auth.py`.

`deployed` IS NOT SETTABLE HERE. The controller knows when a build finished; it
does not decide the app should take traffic. That is promote, a separate act
by the builder. Collapsing them would let whichever pod ran the build put an
app in front of users.

409 on an illegal transition rather than a silent no-op, so a controller that
reports out of order learns it rather than leaving a deployment wedged in a
state nobody wrote.

404 for an unknown deployment, and 404 for a wrong or absent controller token,
deliberately indistinguishable. The controller is not a tenant and has no org,
so there is no ownership check to make here: the deployment id is resolved
against the control plane rather than trusted, and it is the only thing this
credential can act on.

Promote a built deployment to serve traffic.

409 when the state machine forbids it -- a deployment cannot become
`deployed` without having been built, and a `failed` one cannot be revived.

Roll back a deployment that is currently serving.

Only a `deployed` deployment may be rolled back. Rolling back one that never
served is meaningless, and permitting it would let a builder mark a failed
build `rolled_back` and hide the failure.

get.description:
Why a build failed.

Returns every step of the build pod in the order Kubernetes runs them --
fetch, scan-source, build, scan-image, then push -- because "which step" is
most of the answer. A step that has not started is omitted rather than
returned empty, so a build in progress reports what exists so far.

An empty `containers` list means the build pod is gone or was never created.
Build pods are reaped an hour after they finish (`ttlSecondsAfterFinished`),
so logs for an older deployment are genuinely unavailable rather than hidden;
`last_error_sanitized` on the deployment is what survives.

`redacted` is always true and means graph8's credential patterns were applied.
It is NOT a claim the output is safe to publish: this is a customer's own
build output and it can print a secret in a shape no pattern matches.
